1.

In this appeal, the appellant seeks a direction from this Court to set aside the impugned nil award dated 11.12.2024 passed by the Railway Claims Tribunal, Bhubaneswar in O.A. No.32 of 2023 and to grant statutory compensation for the death of the deceased caused in an untoward railway incident under Section 124-A of the Railways Act, 1989.

sentences.text: Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK I.

FACTUAL MATRIX OF THE CASE:
2.

The brief facts of the caseare asfollows:
(i) On the night of 23.11.2022, the deceased, Sarat Chandra Kar, was stated to have been travelling by Train No. 18410, Sri Jagannath Express, from JJKR Railway Station towards Howrah Railway Station.

It was alleged that while the train was passing near Ranital Railway Station at Km No.
288/28-26, he fell from the moving train and sustained injuries, and that he died on 24.11.2022.
The deceased was found on the down line track at the said location with severe injuries.

(ii) The Railway materials record that during inquest proceedings no journey ticket or travel authority was recovered from the person of the deceased, and they also note that there was no direct eyewitness to the alleged fall from the train.
(iii) In connection with the death, Bhadrak GRPS registered a case as U.D. Case No. 77 of 2022 and undertook investigation.
Police proceedings were conducted, including preparation of inquest papers, forwarding of the body for post-mortem examination, and completion of other related formalities.
Documents connected with the said proceedings, including the inquest report, dead body challan, post-mortem report and the final report, form part of the records relied upon in the claim proceedings.

(iv) Subsequently, the mother of the deceased filed OA No. 32 of 2023 before the Railway Claims Tribunal, Bhubaneswar Bench, seeking statutory compensation under the Railways Act, 1989, on the premise that the Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK death resulted from an "untoward incident" and that the deceased was a bona fide passenger.
(v) Upon consideration of the oral and documentary evidence, the Railway Claims Tribunal, by award dated 11.12.2024, rejected the claim and passed a nil award.

The Tribunal recorded findings that the deceased was not established to be a bona fide passenger and that the occurrence was not established to be an "untoward incident" for the purpose of statutory compensation.
Aggrieved by the said award passed in O.A. No. 32 of 2023, the present appeal has been filed.

II. SUBMISSIONS ON BEHALF OF THE APPELLANT:
3. Learned counsel for the Appellant earnestly made the following submissions in support of her contentions:
(i) The appellant submitted that the Tribunal erred in rejecting the claim despite the claimant having placed on record consistent oral and documentary material to show that the deceased was travelling by Train No. 18410, Sri Jagannath Express, from JJKR to Howrah on the night of 23.11.2022 and that he died on 24.11.2022 as a result of an accidental fall from the running train near Ranital Railway Station at Km No.
288/28-26.

It was urged that the police proceedings arising out of Bhadrak GRPS U.D. Case No. 77 of 2022, including the inquest and the final report, support the Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India on 24 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/47075349/
2 occurrence being a case of accidental fall from train, and that the post-mortem and other connected documents are consistent with death due to railway-related injuries.
Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK

sentences.text: (ii) It was further submitted that the Tribunal unjustifiably disbelieved the evidence of A.W.2, the elder brother of the deceased, who deposed that he accompanied the deceased to JJKR Railway Station, witnessed the deceased purchasing a journey ticket for travel to Howrah, and saw him board the said train.

According to the appellant, A.W.2 was cross- examined by the Railway but nothing material was elicited to discredit the core of his testimony, namely, that the deceased travelled by the said train and suffered fatal injuries in the course of that journey.

The appellant contended that in the absence of any credible rebuttal evidence, the testimony of A.W.2, read with the contemporaneous police records, was sufficient to establish that the deceased was a bona fide passenger and that the occurrence constituted an untoward incident.

(iii) The appellant also submitted that the Railway's witness, R.W.1, being an RPF personnel associated with the enquiry, was not an eyewitness to the occurrence and his testimony could not displace the inference arising from the inquest and police final report.

Emphasis was placed on the proposition that non-recovery of the journey ticket from the deceased is not determinative of the issue of bona fide passenger status, particularly where the surrounding facts and evidence corroborate travel and accidental fall.

In this regard, reliance was placed on the decision of the Supreme Court in Doli Rani Saha v. Union of India (Civil Appeal No. 8605 of 2021, disposed of on 09.08.2024), to contend that absence of the ticket does not defeat a claim if the relevant facts Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK establish the incident, and that where the claimant's version of travel is not effectively rebutted, bona fide passenger status can be inferred.

sentences.text: (iv) It was lastly submitted that once the occurrence is shown to fall within the statutory description of an untoward incident, compensation under Section 124-A follows as a rule, subject only to the limited exceptions in the proviso, and that the Tribunal erred in introducing a possibility of exceptions without the Railway establishing the same on evidence.

On these submissions, the appellant urged that the impugned nil award be set aside and compensation be granted in accordance with the Railway Accidents and Untoward Incidents (Compensation) Rules, 1990. III.

SUBMISSIONS ADVANCED ON BEHALF OF THE RESPONDENT:
4. Learned counsel for the Respondent earnestly made the following submissions in support of her contentions:
(i) The respondents submitted that the learned Tribunal rightly dismissed the claim on merits after assessing the pleadings, records and evidence from both sides.

It was contended that the appellant failed to discharge the initial burden of proving the foundational requirements for compensation, namely that the deceased was travelling as a bona fide passenger by Train No. 18410 on the strength of a valid ticket/travel authority and that the occurrence was an "untoward incident" under Section 123(c) read with Section 124-A of the Railways Act, 1989.

The respondents Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India on 24 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/47075349/
3 asserted that there was no reliable material to support the allegation of jerk or accidental fall, and that the on-duty Guard of the train had stated during enquiry that the train passed the Bhadrak- Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK Ranital Link Junction Cabin section safely, without any report of an untoward incident or abnormal jerk.

entities.text: Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: (ii) The respondents further argued that the Tribunal correctly disbelieved the testimony of AW-2 (elder brother of the deceased) because his deposition before the Tribunal was inconsistent with his earlier statement recorded during the Railway enquiry, particularly on whether he actually saw the ticket purchase and boarding, and on the time when he left the station.

According to the respondents, these contradictions went to the root of the appellant's attempt to prove ticket purchase and bona fide passenger status, and justified treating AW-2 as an interested witness whose version could not be relied upon.
(iii) It was also submitted that no journey ticket was recovered during inquest, no luggage was found, and there was no eyewitness to the alleged fall.

The body was noticed only later by the trackman inside the track, and the respondents contended that the inquest report and police final report were not conclusive proof of an accidental fall from a train, but at best presumptive.
They submitted that the post-mortem report did not certify that the deceased was a passenger or that death occurred due to a fall from a running train.

On law, reliance was placed on the principle in Union of India v. Rina Devi1 that mere presence of a body on railway premises is not conclusive to establish bona fide passenger status, and that only after the claimant establishes the basic ingredients does the burden shift to the Railways.

IV. ANALYSIS OF THE IMPUGNED JUDGMENT:
5. The Tribunal dismissed the claim on merits, holding against the applicant on the principal issues of (i) bona fide passenger status, (ii) whether the death resulted from an "untoward incident" under Section 123(c)(2) read with Section 124-A of the Railways Act, 1989, and (iii) the consequent entitlement to statutory compensation.
It found that the material on record did not establish that the deceased was travelling with a valid journey ticket or that his death was caused by an accidental fall from a running train.

On that basis, the Tribunal held that no compensation under Section 124-A was payable, and having answered issues 1 to 3 against the applicant, it did not examine issues 4 and 5 relating to dependency and relief.
6. In reaching this conclusion, the Tribunal first scrutinised the oral evidence.

It noted that the applicant (AW-1) was not a co-passenger and had not witnessed the occurrence, nor had she visited the spot or hospital, and that her deposition essentially reiterated what was pleaded.

The Tribunal then examined the evidence of the deceased's elder brother (AW-2), who was relied upon to prove purchase of ticket Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India on 24 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/47075349/
4 and boarding of the train.

entities.text: Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Tribunal compared AW-2's deposition before the Bench (including his affidavit and cross-examination) with his earlier statement recorded by the RPF as part of the Railway's investigation materials.

It found material inconsistencies regarding the Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK timing and sequence of events, particularly as to whether AW-2 remained at the station until the train's arrival and departure or had left earlier in the evening after handing over food items.

On that basis, the Tribunal treated AW-2 as an "interested witness" and held that his version did not inspire confidence and could not be relied upon to establish the ticket purchase/boarding narrative.
7. The Tribunal next relied upon the contemporaneous official records and surrounding circumstances.

It noted that the first information within the Railway system was a station diary entry based on the report of the on- duty trackman, who noticed the dead body inside the down line track at the identified kilometre location in the morning hours.

The Tribunal recorded that, as per the spot-related materials, the body was found inside the track and the injuries were described as extremely severe, including severance of the head from the body and both hands being cut from the shoulders.
It also treated as significant the fact that no journey ticket or travel authority was recovered during the inquest and that no luggage was found near the spot.

The Tribunal further observed that there was no direct eyewitness to an accidental fall and that there was no report of any such falling incident from the on-duty crew/managerial staff of the alleged train until the body was noticed by the trackman.

8. On a cumulative assessment, the Tribunal reasoned that the location of the body inside the track,
the nature of the injuries as reflected in the post-mortem report, the absence of ticket recovery, and the absence of Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK
direct or supportive evidence of a fall from a running train together created a preponderance of probability against the claim version.

While it noticed that the police final report contained a remark attributing death to fall from a train,
the Tribunal held that such remark was not supported by direct or corroborative evidence sufficient to establish the statutory ingredients.

It therefore concluded that the applicant had not proved bona fide passenger status or an untoward incident and added that there was "every possibility" that the death could have arisen due to one of the exceptions under the proviso (a) to (c) of Section 124-A.

Consequently, the claim was dismissed V. COURT'S REASONING AND ANALYSIS:
9. Heard Learned Counsel for the parties and perused the documents placed before this Court.
10. The appellant (mother of the deceased) challenges the Railway Claims Tribunal's award which denied compensation for the death of her son.
The Tribunal's findings were that the deceased was not proved to be a bona fide passenger and that the death was not shown to result from an "untoward incident" under the Railways Act, 1989.
The task before this Court is to re-appreciate the evidence and legal standards governing such claims to determine whether the appellant is entitled to compensation.

entities.text: Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India on 24 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Under Section 124-A of the Railways Act, 1989, the railway administration is strictly liable to pay compensation for death or injury
Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK caused to a passenger by an "untoward incident", which includes an accidental fall from a train (Section 123(c)(2)).
This liability is based on a no-fault principle and the negligence of the victim is immaterial.
12. The only defences available to the Railways are the narrow exceptions listed in the proviso to Section 124-A such as self-inflicted injury, suicide or criminal trespass by the victim.
Unless the Railways establish that the case falls within those exceptions, compensation must be paid for an untoward incident causing a passenger's death or injury.

In other words, if a bona fide passenger suffers a mishap like an accidental fall from a train, the Railways are liable to compensate, and contributory negligence (for instance, carelessness in boarding or traveling) is not a bar to the claim.
This legislative scheme, being part of a social welfare statute, must be applied in a spirit that favors the victims where appropriate.

13. To this effect, the Supreme Court in the case of Rina Devi(Supra) held as follows:
"We are unable to uphold the above view as the concept of 'self inflicted injury' would require intention to inflict such injury and not mere negligence of any particular degree.
Doing so would amount to invoking the principle of contributory negligence which cannot be done in the case of liability based on 'no fault theory'.

We may in this connection refer to judgment of this Court in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. versus Sunil Kumar laying down that plea of negligence of the victim cannot be allowed in claim based on 'no fault theory' under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

entities.text: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. versus Sunil Kumar
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Accordingly, we hold that death or injury in the course of boarding or de-boarding a train will Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK be an 'untoward incident'
entitling a victim to the compensation and will not fall under the proviso to Section 124A merely on the plea of negligence of the victim as a contributing factor."
14.

The claimant must first establish on a balance of probabilities that the victim was a bona fide passenger (i.e. traveling with a valid ticket or authority) and that the injury or death was caused by an untoward incident.
There was some divergence in judicial opinions on how strictly this initial burden lies on the claimant.

he Supreme Court in Rina Devi (Supra) resolved this by holding that while the mere presence of a body on railway premises is not by itself conclusive proof of bona fide travel, the mere absence of a ticket on the body will not negate a compensation claim if other evidence suggests that the person had indeed been traveling.

15. The initial onus can be discharged by the claimant through credible evidence such as eyewitness testimony or affidavits of relevant facts, and once that is done, the burden shifts to the Railways to rebut the claim or to prove that an exception applies.
In Rina Devi, it was succinctly held that mere absence of a ticket would not negate the claim that the deceased was a bona fide passenger.
The claimant's version, if supported by attending circumstances, gives rise to a presumption in favor of bona fide travel, which the Railways must then disprove by concrete evidence.
The relevant excerpts are produced below:

6

entities.text: Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India on 24 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "We thus hold that mere presence of a body on the Railway premises will not be conclusive to hold that injured or deceased was a bona fide passenger for which claim for Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK compensation could be maintained.
However, mere absence of ticket with such injured or deceased will not negative the claim that he was a bona fide passenger.

Initial burden will be on the claimant which can be discharged by filing an affidavit of the relevant facts and burden will then shift on the Railways and the issue can be decided on the facts shown or the attending circumstances.
This will have to be dealt with from case to case on the basis of facts found.
The legal position in this regard will stand explained accordingly."

16. The appellant's case is that her son was travelling on the night of 23.11.2022 by Train No. 18410 Sri Jagannath Express from Jajpur Keonjhar Road towards Howrah and accidentally fell from the moving train near Km. 288/28 to 26 close to Ranital Station.
He sustained grievous injuries and died on 24.11.2022.

To support this version, the appellant relies on the testimony of the deceased's elder brother examined as A.W.2, who stated that he accompanied the deceased to the station,
helped him purchase a second class ticket up to Howrah, saw him board the train, and handed over the ticket to him before departure.

17. The appellant also produced records from Bhadrak GRPS U.D. Case No. 77 of 2022, including the inquest report, post mortem report, and final report, wherein the police, upon investigation,
recorded the death as a case of accidental fall from a train.

It is undisputed that the body was found on the railway track at the stated location in the early hours of 24.11.2022 by a patrolman, though no ticket or luggage was recovered Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK from the person of the deceased.
The police investigation did not reveal any prior enmity, foul play, or any non railway cause for the death.
18. The Claims Tribunal was not satisfied that the deceased was a bona fide passenger or that the death resulted from an accidental fall.
It relied mainly on two circumstances.
First, it found A.W.2's evidence unreliable.

Second, it treated the condition of the body and the absence of ticket or luggage as suggesting an alternative possibility, including that the deceased may have been run over on the tracks without travelling in the train.
These aspects have been reconsidered in light of the governing principles.
19. A.W.2, being the brother of the deceased, is an interested witness and his testimony must be tested with care.
He stated that he escorted the deceased to the station and saw him board the train with a purchased ticket.
In cross examination, a discrepancy emerged between his deposition before the Tribunal and his earlier statement to the RPF.

In the RPF statement, he appeared to suggest that he left earlier after arranging food and water, whereas before the Tribunal he indicated that he remained until the train arrived and saw the deceased depart.
This contradiction bears on whether A.W.2 actually witnessed the boarding and departure, and the Tribunal therefore rejected his version.
20. This Court finds that A.W.2's versions are not fully consistent on that limited aspect.

However,
he has remained consistent on the central narrative that the deceased intended to travel by the Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India on 24 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/47075349/
7 Jagannath Express and that a ticket was procured for that journey.

entities.text: Rukmani Kar vs Union Of India
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There is no material Location:
ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK suggesting any independent reason for the deceased to be on the tracks otherwise.
The body was found along the same route near an intermediate station in the early hours, which is broadly consistent with the travel version.
In a claim under Section 124A, the Court must avoid an unduly technical approach that defeats the object of beneficial legislation.
If the claimant's version is reasonably probable and is not displaced by reliable contrary evidence, it should not be rejected merely due to minor inconsistencies.
21. The respondents suggested that the case may fall within the proviso to Section 124A, such as suicide, self-inflicted injury, or trespass.
No evidence was led to support any such plea.
There is nothing on record to indicate suicidal intent, deliberate self-harm, or any criminal act.
The theory that the deceased was merely on the track at night and was run over is speculative and unsupported by any material.

The unrebutted case of the family is that he was travelling to Howrah for a purpose,
which makes the travel narrative more probable.
Once the claimant establishes a prima facie case of accidental falling of a passenger, the burden shifts to the Railways to prove that an exception applies.
That burden has not been discharged.

A bare suggestion of possibilities cannot defeat a claim under Section 124A.
VI. CONCLUSION:
22.
For these reasons, the impugned award is set aside and the appeal is allowed.
This Court holds that the death occurred due to an untoward incident while the deceased was a passenger on the train in question.
Location: ORISSA HIGH COURT, CUTTACK
The appellant is entitled to statutory compensation of 8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight Lakhs) under the Railway Accidents and Untoward Incidents (Compensation) Rules, 1990, as amended.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The respondent shall pay the said amount with interest at 6% per annum from 23.11.2022 till payment, within three months from today.

23. The Tribunal is directed to release 50% of the awarded amount to the Appellant by way of account transfer or cheque and the rest of the amount to be kept in an interest bearing fixed deposit account for a period of three years or subject to the order of the Tribunal.
24. Interim order, if any, passed earlier stands vacated.
